entries.meaning: Rāma lovingly lifted the young ascetic and embraced him with thrilling joy. It seemed, everyone said, that embodied Love and the highest spiritual Reality had met. The ascetic then touched Lakṣmaṇa's feet; Lakṣmaṇa raised him, overflowing with affection. Next he placed the dust of Sītā's feet upon his head, regarding her as his mother, and received her blessing like a child. He bowed to the Niṣāda as well, and Guha joyfully met him on seeing that he loved Rāma. Drinking the nectar of the divine form through the cups of his eyes, the ascetic rejoiced like a hungry man who has gained excellent food. Meanwhile the men and women, gazing upon the beauty of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā, were overcome by affection and asked what kind of parents could have sent such children to the woods. Raghu's hero instructed his friend Guha in many ways; placing Rāma's command upon his head, Guha then departed for home.

Sītā, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa again joined their hands and bowed to the Yamunā. Sītā with them, the two brothers went on gladly, praising the daughter of the Sun. Many travelers met them on the road and, seeing the brothers, spoke with love: royalty marks every limb of yours, yet our hearts ache to see you walking the road on foot; by our reckoning, astrology is false. The path is inaccessible, crowded with mountains and dense forest, and you have a delicate woman with you. Fierce lions and elephants roam there; if you command, we shall accompany you, conduct you as far as needed, and then return after bowing our heads. Again and again people asked in this way under love's power, bodies thrilled and eyes wet. The ocean of compassion gently turned them back with humble words.

The gods envied every town and village along the road: what meritorious person had founded them at what blessed hour, so fortunate and filled with holiness? Wherever Rāma's feet traveled was the equal of no celestial city. Even heaven's residents praised the people who dwelt beside that store of merit, the road. Those who filled their eyes with cloud-dark Rāma together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa were blessed, as were the lakes and rivers in which he bathed. If the lord sat beneath a tree, the wish-fulfilling trees acclaimed it. The earth counted its own fortune immense when touched by pollen from Rāma's lotus feet. Clouds cast shade, hosts of gods rained flowers and voiced their admiration, and as Rāma continued along the road the mountains, forests, birds, and beasts gazed upon him.

Whenever Raghu's lord came near a village with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, all its children, elders, men, and women immediately left their household work and went out. Gazing at Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā's beauty, they gained the fruit of their eyes and became joyful. Eyes wet and bodies thrilled, all were absorbed in seeing the two heroes. Their state cannot be described: it was as though paupers had discovered a heap of celestial jewels. Calling one another, they urged everyone to seize this brief reward for the eyes. Some, captivated at the sight of Rāma, continued walking behind him. Others carried the road's image into eyes and heart, then stood weak in body, mind, and speech. Some saw a fine banyan's shade, spread soft grass and leaves, and begged the travelers not to waste their fatigue: should they set out again after a moment's rest, or in the morning?

Some brought jars filled with water and gently invited their lord to drink. Hearing their loving words and seeing such devotion, gracious and exceptionally well-mannered Rāma recognized Sītā's weariness and delayed for a little while beneath a banyan. Glad men and women gazed upon the incomparable beauty that enticed both eyes and mind. All stood fixed around him like cakora birds before Rāmacandra's moonlike face. His youthful body, dark as a tamāla tree, shone with beauty that could entrance millions of Cupids. Fair-complexioned Lakṣmaṇa looked exceedingly fine, handsome from toenail to crown and dear to the heart. Ascetic cloth was bound around their waists, quivers hung there, and bow and arrows graced their lotus-like hands. Lovely crowns of matted hair adorned their heads; broad chests, long arms, and great eyes shone beneath faces like the full autumn moon, now netted with beads of sweat.

That captivating pair cannot be described: my understanding is slight and their beauty immense. Everyone fixed heart, mind, and intellect upon Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā's loveliness. Men and women, thirsty with love, stood transfixed like a doe and buck gazing upon their two fawns. Village women went close to Sītā and, although deeply affectionate, asked their question shyly. Again and again they touched her feet and spoke in their gentle, guileless nature: Princess, we make a request, though as women we fear to ask. Mistress, forgive our discourtesy and do not take it amiss, knowing us to be simple villagers. These two princes are naturally charming; from them emerald and gold have borrowed their radiance. One is dark and one fair, noble youths, embodiments of beauty; their faces are autumn moons and their eyes autumn lotuses.

Fair-faced lady, they put millions of Cupids to shame—tell us, who are they to you? Hearing the lovely, affectionate question, Sītā felt shy and smiled inwardly. Looking toward the women and then down at the ground, lovely-complexioned Sītā grew bashful at both their and her own reserve. The young, doe-eyed princess, shy yet loving, spoke sweetly in a cuckoo-like voice: the fair one is naturally handsome, and his name is Lakṣmaṇa, my younger brother-in-law. Then she covered her moonlike face with the edge of her garment, glanced toward her beloved's body, and crooked her eyebrows. Through a charming sidelong look from wagtail-like eyes, Sītā silently indicated her husband to them. All the village women rejoiced as though paupers had plundered a royal treasure. Falling at Sītā's feet with great love, they gave many blessings: may you remain married as long as the earth rests upon the serpent's head.

May you be dear to your husband as Pārvatī is, they said; goddess, do not withdraw your kindness from us. With hands joined they repeatedly pleaded that, if Sītā ever returned by this road, she remember them as servants and grant them another sight. Sītā saw that all were thirsty for love and satisfied them with repeated sweet words, like moonlight nourishing water lilies. Lakṣmaṇa then understood Rāma's intention and gently asked the people for the road. Men and women grew sorrowful at hearing him; bodies thrilled and eyes filled with tears. Their joy vanished and their minds darkened, as though Fate had bestowed a treasure only to snatch it away. Understanding the course of karma, they took courage, carefully found the easy road, and described it. Raghunātha then departed with Lakṣmaṇa and Jānakī, turning everyone back with loving words while carrying their hearts along.

As the men and women returned, they bitterly regretted the parting and inwardly blamed the gods. They told one another in grief that all Fate's works were inverted. Utterly unrestrained, cruel, and fearless, Fate had made the moon diseased and marked with a stain, trees rough and the ocean salty—and had now sent the princes to the forest. If it meant to give these three forest exile, its creation of worldly pleasures was wasted. They wandered barefoot on the road, so Fate's making of many vehicles was vain. They lay upon earth spread with kuśa grass and leaves; why, then, had the Creator fashioned beautiful beds? Fate had assigned them the shelter of great trees, so all the labor of repeatedly creating white palaces had been for nothing.

If these three eat roots and fruits, one villager said, then nectar and every refined food in the world were made in vain. Another said they were beautiful by their own nature, self-manifest rather than fashioned by the Creator. As far as the Vedas speak of Fate's workmanship and as far as ear, eye, and mind can apprehend and describe it, search all fourteen worlds: where is a man like this, where a woman like her? Seeing them, Brahmā's mind became enamored and he began to make a worthy comparison, but despite great effort no equal appeared; out of jealousy he brought them away and hid them in the forest. Others admitted they knew little and simply counted themselves supremely blessed. Those who saw them, will see them, or have seen those who saw them were all stores of merit. Speaking such loving words with eyes brimming, the villagers wondered how bodies so exceedingly tender would travel the inaccessible road.
